summary.text: Write the digit sum as \(s(n)=2^a5^bq\) with \(\gcd(q,10)=1\), set \(t=\varphi(q)\), and use \(n\equiv s(n)\pmod 9\) to choose \(0\le j<q\) such that \(q\mid n+9j\). Construct \(k\) from \(n-j\) length-\(t\) decimal blocks representing \(1\), \(j\) length-\(2t\) blocks representing \(10\), and \(n\) trailing zeros; then \(s(k)=n\), Euler’s theorem and the zeros give \(s(n)\mid k\), and \(k\ge 10^n>n\), so \(k\) is a distinct amicable partner.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(x)\) denote the sum of the decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\). We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has a positive integer \(k\ne n\) such that
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
This will show that the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is nonempty; since all its members are positive, its least member is positive and hence \(a(n)\ne0\).

We use the following notation for decimal digit words. If
\[
W=(w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_{r-1})
\]
is a finite list of digits, written in least-significant-digit-first order, put
\[
[W]_{10}=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}w_i10^i.
\]
If every \(w_i\) lies between \(0\) and \(9\), then the decimal digit sum of \([W]_{10}\) is \(\sum_iw_i\). The only possible discrepancy between the word and the usual decimal representation is the deletion of zeroes at the high-order end, and that does not change the digit sum. Also, for concatenated words \(U,V\),
\[
[U V]_{10}=[U]_{10}+10^{|U|}[V]_{10}. \tag{1}
\]

Fix \(n>0\), and set
\[
d=D(n).
\]
Two standard properties of decimal digit sums are
\[
1\le d\le n \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
n\equiv d\pmod 9. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, a positive integer has at least one nonzero decimal digit, giving \(d>0\); the inequality \(D(n)\le n\) is the usual digit-sum bound; and (3) follows from \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\).

Separate from \(d\) all factors of \(2\) and \(5\). Thus there are nonnegative integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(d'\) such that
\[
d=2^a5^b d',\qquad \gcd(d',10)=1. \tag{4}
\]
Let
\[
t=\varphi(d').
\]
This is positive. Euler's theorem gives
\[
10^t\equiv1\pmod{d'}. \tag{5}
\]
For \(d'=1\), the congruence is of course automatic, so this statement covers that case as well.

We next choose an integer \(j\) satisfying
\[
0\le j<d',\qquad d'\mid n+9j. \tag{6}
\]
To see that such a \(j\) exists, let \(g=\gcd(9,d')\). Since \(d'\mid d\), we have \(g\mid d\). Moreover, (3) says that \(9\mid n-d\), and \(g\mid9\), so \(g\mid n\). The standard solvability criterion for a linear congruence therefore shows that
\[
9j\equiv -n\pmod{d'}
\]
has a solution: the congruence \(Ax\equiv B\pmod M\) is solvable precisely when \(\gcd(A,M)\mid B\). Taking the least nonnegative residue of a solution gives (6).

We will need that \(j\le n\). From (4), \(d'\mid d\), and since both are positive, \(d'\le d\). Together with (2) and \(j<d'\), this yields
\[
j<d'\le d\le n, \tag{7}
\]
and in particular \(j\le n\).

We now construct a decimal word. Define two blocks \(P_1\) and \(P_{10}\), again in least-significant-digit-first order, as follows:
\[
P_1=(1,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{t-1}),
\]
so that
\[
|P_1|=t,\qquad [P_1]_{10}=1,\qquad \sum P_1=1, \tag{8}
\]
and
\[
P_{10}=(0,1,\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{2t-2}),
\]
so that
\[
|P_{10}|=2t,\qquad [P_{10}]_{10}=10,\qquad \sum P_{10}=1. \tag{9}
\]
These definitions make sense because \(t\ge1\).

Let \(R\) be the concatenation of \(n-j\) copies of \(P_1\), followed by \(j\) copies of \(P_{10}\). Every block has digit sum \(1\), and there are
\[
(n-j)+j=n
\]
blocks. Consequently,
\[
\sum R=n. \tag{10}
\]

We calculate the numerical value of \(R\) modulo \(d'\). We first record a direct consequence of (1) and (5). If a word \(P\) has length divisible by \(t\), then for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
[\underbrace{P\cdots P}_{m\text{ copies}}]_{10}
   \equiv m[P]_{10}\pmod{d'}. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, when another copy is appended, its positional shift is by a multiple of \(|P|\), and
\(10^{|P|}\equiv1\pmod{d'}\) because \(t\mid |P|\). Induction on the number of copies proves (11).

Apply (11) to the two types of blocks. Since \(|P_1|=t\), the first portion of \(R\), consisting of \(n-j\) copies of \(P_1\), has value congruent to
\[
(n-j)[P_1]_{10}=n-j\pmod{d'}. \tag{12}
\]
Since \(|P_{10}|=2t\), the portion consisting of \(j\) copies of \(P_{10}\) has value congruent to
\[
j[P_{10}]_{10}=10j\pmod{d'}. \tag{13}
\]
The length of the first portion is \((n-j)t\), so the power of \(10\) by which the second portion is shifted is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(d'\), by (5). Hence (1), (12), and (13) give
\[
[R]_{10}\equiv(n-j)+10j=n+9j\equiv0\pmod{d'},
\]
where the last congruence is (6). Thus
\[
d'\mid [R]_{10}. \tag{14}
\]

Now place \(n\) zero digits before \(R\) in least-significant-digit-first order. Let
\[
L=(\underbrace{0,\ldots,0}_{n})R,
\qquad k=[L]_{10}.
\]
By the concatenation formula,
\[
k=10^n[R]_{10}. \tag{15}
\]
The initial zeroes add nothing to the digit sum, so (10) gives
\[
D(k)=n. \tag{16}
\]
In particular, because \(n>0\), this also shows that \(k>0\).

We next prove that \(d\mid k\). It remains only to check that the factor \(10^n\) in (15) contains enough factors of \(2\) and \(5\). From (4), the positive number \(2^a\) divides \(d\), so \(2^a\le d\). Also \(a<2^a\) for every nonnegative integer \(a\). Therefore, using \(d\le n\),
\[
a\le n.
\]
Similarly, \(5^b\mid d\), so \(5^b\le d\), and \(b<5^b\); hence
\[
b\le n.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^a5^b\mid 2^n5^n=10^n. \tag{17}
\]
Combining (14), (15), and (17), we obtain
\[
2^a5^bd'=d\mid 10^n[R]_{10}=k. \tag{18}
\]
Thus the first required divisibility, \(D(n)=d\mid k\), holds. The second follows immediately from (16):
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{19}
\]

It remains to ensure that this partner is distinct from \(n\). Since \(k>0\), equation (15) implies \([R]_{10}>0\). Hence
\[
k=10^n[R]_{10}\ge10^n.
\]
For every nonnegative integer \(n\), and in particular for our positive \(n\), one has
\[
10^n>n
\]
(for example, this follows immediately by induction). Consequently
\[
k\ge10^n>n,
\]
so \(k\ne n\).

We have therefore constructed, for every \(n>0\), a positive integer \(k\) such that
\[
k\ne n,
\qquad D(n)\mid k,
\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
Thus the set of Harshad amicable partners of \(n\) is nonempty. By the well-ordering principle it has a least element, and every element of the set is positive. The sequence value \(a(n)\), defined to be this least partner when partners exist and \(0\) only when none exist, is therefore positive. Hence
\[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every positive integer }n.}
\]
